title: Only 38% Can Spot Their Own Voice on a Recording 🎙️
description:
Why does your voice sound so weird on a recording? When you talk, you hear yourself through the air and through the bones of your skull, which boosts the low tones, but a microphone only picks up the air part, so recordings sound higher and thinner than the voice in your head.

topic: Why does your voice sound so weird on a recording?
script: Only 38 percent of people knew their own voice on a recording. Your skull is why. That's a 1967 study, with five seconds to guess. When you talk, your vocal cords shake the air, and that sound curls around into your ears. But the buzz also takes a shortcut, straight through the bones of your skull. Your skull works like a built-in subwoofer. It boosts the deep tones, so you sound fuller and deeper to yourself. A microphone only catches the air part. No bones, no bass. So the recording sounds higher and thinner, and that's the voice everyone else hears. And in a 2013 study, people rated their own voice more attractive when they didn't know it was theirs. So your voice isn't bad, it's just unfamiliar. Be honest: would you have spotted your own voice?
key_facts: You hear your own voice through air conduction plus bone and tissue conduction; recordings capture only the air part
Bone and tissue conduction enhance lower frequencies, so your voice sounds fuller and deeper to you
In a 1967 study only 38% of people identified recordings of their own voice within 5 seconds
In a 2013 Albright College study of 80 people, participants rated their own voice more attractive when they didn't recognize it
